overall_summary: Space and cosmic anomaly content dominates the channel's performance, particularly extreme planetary environments (e.g., burning ice, coal-dark planets, molten iron rain). Conversely, generic brain and cognitive psychology facts struggle to gain traction, indicating that viewers prefer high-concept cosmic scale and physical paradoxes over internal mental mechanics.

winning_patterns.evidence: 'The Planet of Burning Ice' (1,055 views) and 'The Planet Darker Than Coal' (909 views, 34 likes) are the top performers, showing strong engagement for extreme, hard-to-imagine space conditions.
winning_patterns.action: Double down on extreme exoplanets, cosmic anomalies, and sensory space facts (e.g., what space smells like) using highly descriptive, high-contrast imagery.

winning_patterns.evidence: 'Why Your Head Is Older Than Your Feet' (262 views) and 'Sharks Are Older Than Trees?' (302 views) perform well by challenging the viewer's perception of time and history.
winning_patterns.action: Frame scientific or historical facts as mind-bending timeline clashes or physical paradoxes.

weak_patterns.evidence: 'Your Brain Can Create Fake Memories' (max 52 views) and 'The Real Reason Songs Get Stuck In Your Head' (17 views) consistently underperform.
weak_patterns.action: Avoid standard self-help or basic cognitive psychology facts; pivot to high-stakes mysteries or external cosmic phenomena.

next_video.concept: WASP-12b, the egg-shaped planet being actively eaten by its parent star.
next_video.opening_direction: Show a distorted, egg-shaped planet being violently stretched and stripped of its atmosphere by a glowing star.
next_video.twist_direction: Reveal that this cosmic cannibalism is happening in real-time, and the planet has less than 10 million years before it is completely devoured.
next_video.reason: Leverages the highly successful 'extreme space/planet' formula that drove top views for the burning ice and coal-dark planet videos, utilizing strong visual metaphors of cosmic destruction.

experiment: Test a 'What-If' space scenario focusing on Earth (e.g., 'What If Earth Had Saturn's Rings?') to see if the cosmic anomaly audience translates to localized high-concept space scenarios.
